about: Paper 10, Civil Law in Context, is the Cambridge Law Tripos paper on Roman law, presented by the Faculty as the first advanced legal system, whose principles still underpin much modern law. The Faculty lists its topics as the sources of law in Roman society, ownership and property, contracts, and delict, and explains that it offers a view of a whole legal system in a short time and helps in understanding modern civil-law systems. Roman law has been taught at Cambridge since the Faculty of Law was founded. This pack follows the Faculty's topic list, dividing property, contracts and delict into two topics each.
topics: Roman law as an advanced legal system
Sources of law in Roman society

notes.h: Roman law as an advanced legal system
notes.body:
The Faculty presents Roman law as the first advanced legal system, whose principles still underpin much modern law. Studying it gives a view of a whole legal system in a short time, helps in understanding French, German and other civil-law systems, and shows legal reasoning at work within a society. Roman law has been taught at Cambridge since the Faculty of Law was founded.

A timeline to anchor everything
- Regal period, traditionally 753–509 BC.
- Republic, 509–27 BC. The Twelve Tables (c. 451–450 BC), drafted by a board of ten (the decemviri), were the first written statement of Roman law.
- Principate, from Augustus (27 BC). This was the 'classical' period of the great jurists, roughly the 1st century BC to the early 3rd century AD.
- In AD 212 the Constitutio Antoniniana of Caracalla extended citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
- Later empire (the Dominate, from AD 284). Law came mainly from imperial legislation; the Theodosian Code (438) collected it.

Justinian's codification
Justinian (emperor 527–565), with his minister Tribonian, produced what was later called the Corpus Iuris Civilis:
- the Digest (Pandects), 50 books of extracts from classical jurists, in force from 30 December 533;
- the Institutes, an elementary textbook with the force of law, also of 533, closely modelled on the Institutes of Gaius;
- the Code of imperial constitutions (second edition 534);
- the Novels, Justinian's later legislation.
The name Corpus Iuris Civilis comes from a 16th-century printed edition. Much of what we know of classical law comes through the Digest, so scholars must allow for 'interpolations', changes made by the compilers.

Gaius and the institutional scheme
Gaius' Institutes (c. AD 161) are the only classical legal work to survive substantially intact; the text was rediscovered in a palimpsest in Verona in 1816. Gaius divided all law into persons, things and actions (Gaius 1.8). 'Things' covered property, succession and obligations. This scheme influenced later codes and textbooks across Europe.

Key structural features
- A private law system, built by jurists answering concrete cases rather than by legislation.
- Actions mattered more than rights: in classical procedure you needed a formula (an action) that fitted your facts.
- Persons: the law distinguished free persons and slaves, citizens and non-citizens, and persons independent (sui iuris) and in the power of a paterfamilias (alieni iuris). Slaves were also things (res) owned by others, which matters for the law of delict.

The afterlife of Roman law
- The Digest was rediscovered in Italy in the late 11th century. Teaching at Bologna, associated with Irnerius, began the work of the glossators, culminating in the Glossa ordinaria of Accursius in the 13th century, followed by the commentators (Bartolus, Baldus).
- The 'reception' of Roman law across continental Europe produced the ius commune, a learned law common to much of Europe.
- The great codes drew heavily on Roman law: the French Code civil (1804) and the German BGB (in force 1900). Scots law and Roman-Dutch law (in South Africa) remain openly influenced by it.
- English common law developed separately, but concepts such as the classification of obligations and many maxims have Roman roots.

Why it matters in the exam
Questions often ask you to evaluate whether Roman law was 'advanced' or 'modern'. Good answers use specific institutions: consensual contracts based on agreement alone; good faith (bona fides) as a standard in judicial assessment; an objective concept of fault (culpa) in the lex Aquilia; the protection of possession independent of ownership; and a sophisticated method of reasoning from cases. They also note what is alien to us: slavery, patria potestas, and penal actions for delict.

Exam tips: anchor every answer in specific texts and institutions with approximate dates, and distinguish classical law from Justinian's law.

notes.h: Sources of law in Roman society
notes.body:
Roman law was produced by several different sources at different periods. Gaius (1.2) lists them as statutes (leges), plebiscites, resolutions of the senate, imperial constitutions, the edicts of magistrates and the opinions of jurists.

Statutes and plebiscites
- Leges were passed by assemblies of the Roman people on a magistrate's proposal.
- Plebiscita were resolutions of the plebeian assembly. The lex Hortensia (287 BC) made them binding on all citizens, and much private law legislation, including the lex Aquilia, took this form.
- Statute was relatively unimportant for private law compared with the edict and the jurists.

Senatusconsulta
Resolutions of the senate were originally advisory. Under the Principate they came to have the force of law, for example the senatusconsultum Macedonianum (1st century AD), which made loans of money to sons in power unenforceable.

The edict of the praetor
- The praetor urbanus (created 367 BC) and the praetor peregrinus (c. 242 BC, for cases involving foreigners) controlled access to the courts.
- At the start of his year of office the praetor published an edict saying which actions, defences (exceptiones) and remedies he would grant. Successive praetors carried most clauses forward.
- Through the edict the praetors created new remedies, such as the actio Publiciana and actions for fraud, and good-faith actions. Papinian described praetorian law as introduced to aid, supplement or correct the civil law in the public interest.
- Under Hadrian the jurist Salvius Julianus settled the text of the edict (c. AD 130), after which it could no longer be freely changed.
- The curule aediles, who supervised markets, issued their own edict, important for latent defects in sale.

The resulting categories
- Ius civile: the law of Roman citizens, from statute, custom and interpretation.
- Ius honorarium: law from the magistrates' edicts.
- Ius gentium: law thought common to all peoples, applied also to foreigners (e.g. the consensual contracts, traditio).
- Ius naturale: law of nature, a philosophical idea often used interchangeably with ius gentium.

The jurists
Jurists were legal experts who gave opinions (responsa), advised magistrates and parties, and wrote commentaries and textbooks.
- Augustus granted some jurists the ius respondendi, the right to give opinions with the emperor's authority.
- Two schools, the Sabinians and the Proculians, disagreed on many questions (e.g. specificatio and whether barter is sale).
- The leading late classical jurists were Papinian, Paul and Ulpian; Ulpian and Paul together supply a large share of the Digest.
- The Law of Citations (AD 426) told judges to follow the majority opinion of Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Modestinus and Gaius, with Papinian prevailing on a tie.

Imperial constitutions
The emperor made law through edicts, decrees (judgments), rescripts (written answers to petitions or officials) and mandates (instructions to officials). By the later empire legislation was the dominant source.

Procedure
- Legis actiones: the earliest, highly formal procedure; a mistake in words could lose the case.
- Formulary procedure: introduced by the lex Aebutia (2nd century BC) and the leges Iuliae (17 BC). The case was set up before the praetor (in iure), who granted a written formula, and then tried before a lay judge (iudex) appointed by the parties. Parts of a formula include the demonstratio (describing the transaction), the intentio (the claim), the condemnatio (authority to condemn or absolve) and sometimes an exceptio (defence).
- Cognitio: under the empire, an official heard the whole case; it gradually replaced the formulary system, which was abolished in the 4th century.
Roman law was therefore 'law of actions': a right existed in practice if there was an action to enforce it.

Exam tips: show how the praetor and the jurists, rather than legislation, drove legal development, and use one or two concrete examples, such as new praetorian remedies or the Sabinian–Proculian disputes.

Ownership (dominium) was the fullest right over a thing. Roman law distinguished it sharply from possession, and the rules for transferring it depended on the kind of thing involved.

Classification of things
- Res mancipi: land and buildings on Italian soil, slaves, oxen, horses, mules and donkeys, and rustic praedial servitudes. These were the key assets of an early farming society.
- Res nec mancipi: everything else, including money and most movables.
- Other divisions: corporeal and incorporeal things (e.g. rights, inheritances), and things outside commerce (sacred places, public things).

Modes of transfer
- Mancipatio: a formal ceremony for res mancipi, in the presence of at least five adult Roman citizens as witnesses and a scale-holder (libripens). The transferee grasped the thing, declared it his, and struck the scale with a piece of bronze.
- In iure cessio: a collusive lawsuit before the praetor, in which the transferee claimed the thing and the owner did not contest. It could be used for res mancipi and nec mancipi, and for incorporeal things.
- Traditio: informal delivery of possession with a lawful ground (iusta causa), such as sale or gift. It transferred ownership of res nec mancipi.
- Justinian's Institutes (2.1.41): in a sale, ownership passed on delivery only once the price was paid or secured, or credit given.

Bonitary ownership
If a res mancipi was simply delivered by traditio, civil-law ownership did not pass. The praetor protected the recipient, who was said to have the thing 'in bonis':
- against the transferor's claim, by the exceptio rei venditae et traditae;
- against third parties, by the actio Publiciana, which treated him as if usucapio had been completed.
After the usucapio period he became full civil owner. Justinian abolished the distinction between res mancipi and nec mancipi in AD 531, and mancipatio had fallen out of use, so traditio became the general mode of transfer.

Usucapio (acquisition by possession over time)
The Twelve Tables set the periods at two years for land and one year for other things. The later learning summarised the requirements as:
- res habilis: a thing capable of usucapio (not stolen or taken by force: stolen things were excluded by the Twelve Tables and the lex Atinia);
- titulus: a lawful ground (iusta causa), such as purchase;
- fides: good faith at the start of possession;
- possessio: actual possession;
- tempus: the required time.
Justinian set the periods at three years for movables and ten years (between parties in the same province) or twenty years (otherwise) for land.
Usucapio cured defects in title, for example a purchase from a non-owner or a defective form of transfer.

Protecting ownership
- Rei vindicatio: the owner's action to recover his thing from whoever possessed it. The claimant had to prove ownership, which could be difficult; usucapio eased this.
- Actio Publiciana: protection for the bonitary owner, and for a good-faith purchaser from a non-owner while usucapio is running (though the latter could not defeat the true owner).
- Actio negatoria: denying that the defendant had a servitude over the owner's land.

Worked example
A sells a horse (res mancipi) to B, receives the price, and simply hands it over. In classical law B is not civil owner (no mancipatio), but holds it in bonis. If A later claims it, B has the exceptio rei venditae et traditae. If a thief takes it, B can sue with the actio Publiciana. After one year's possession, B becomes full owner by usucapio.

Exam tips: always identify the type of thing (res mancipi or nec mancipi), the mode of transfer used, and whether usucapio could cure a defect. Distinguish classical from Justinianic rules.

Besides derivative transfer, Roman law recognised 'natural' or original modes of acquiring ownership, which Justinian's Institutes (Book 2, title 1) discuss through vivid examples. It also protected possession as such, and recognised limited rights over another's property.

Occupatio
A thing belonging to no one (res nullius) becomes the property of the first taker.
- Wild animals, birds and fish belong to whoever catches them, even on another's land, though the landowner may forbid entry.
- Ownership is lost if the animal regains its natural freedom: it escapes from sight or can be pursued only with difficulty.
- A wounded wild animal: Trebatius thought it belonged to the hunter while he kept up the pursuit, but the prevailing view, adopted by Justinian, was that it becomes his only when actually caught.
- Tamed animals that habitually go and return (e.g. peacocks, pigeons) remain owned while they keep the habit of returning.
- Treasure: by a rule attributed to Hadrian, treasure found on one's own land belongs to the finder; treasure found by chance on another's land is shared half to the finder and half to the landowner.

Accessio
A thing joined to another, principal thing becomes part of it.
- Superficies solo cedit: what is built on land belongs to the landowner. A building made with another's materials belongs to the landowner, but the materials' owner had an action (actio de tigno iuncto, from the Twelve Tables) for double value, and could vindicate the materials if the building came down.
- Writing on another's parchment belongs to the owner of the parchment, even if in gold letters.
- Painting on another's board: Justinian held that the board goes with the painting, as it would be absurd for a painting by Apelles or Parrhasius to become an accessory of a cheap board; compensation is payable.
- Alluvion (gradual deposits by a river) belongs to the riparian owner; an island arising in a river belongs to the owners of the adjoining banks.

Specificatio
When someone makes a new thing (nova species) from another's materials, who owns it?
- Sabinians: the owner of the materials.
- Proculians: the maker.
- Justinian's 'middle view': if the thing can be returned to its former materials (e.g. a bronze vase can be melted down), it belongs to the owner of the materials; if not (wine from grapes, a ship from planks), it belongs to the maker. If the maker used partly his own materials, he owns the product.

Mixtures
Confusio (liquids) or commixtio (solids) by consent creates common ownership; where solids such as grain are mixed by accident, each owner in principle keeps his own and can claim a proportionate share.

Possession
Possession is factual control with the intention to possess: Paul says we acquire possession by body and mind (corpore et animo).
- It is protected by the praetor's interdicts regardless of title: uti possidetis (land), utrubi (movables), unde vi (recovery after forcible ejection).
- Borrowers, depositees and hirers held only 'natural possession' (detention) and had no interdicts; exceptionally, the pledge creditor and the holder by grant at will (precario) were protected.
- Possession is also the basis of usucapio.

Servitudes
Servitudes are rights over another's property.
- Praedial servitudes benefit a piece of land (the dominant tenement) at the expense of a neighbouring servient tenement. Rustic examples are rights of way (iter, actus, via) and rights to draw water (aquae ductus). Urban examples are rights of support, light and to prevent building higher. A servitude cannot oblige the servient owner to do anything positive.
- Personal servitudes benefit a person. Usufruct, the right to use another's thing and take its fruits without impairing its substance, ends at the latest on the holder's death; usus and habitatio are narrower.

Exam tips: in problem questions, test each rival claimant against occupatio, accessio and specificatio in turn, and say whether the Sabinian, Proculian or Justinianic view is being applied.

notes.h: Contracts: the system, real and verbal contracts
notes.body:
Roman law did not have a general law of contract in the modern sense. It had a law of contracts: a list of specific types, each with its own requirements and action. An agreement that fitted no type was generally unenforceable.

Obligations
Justinian's Institutes define an obligation as a legal bond by which we are bound by necessity to perform something according to the laws of our state. Gaius divides obligations into those arising from contract and those from delict, and classifies contracts by how they are formed (Gaius 3.89):
- re (by delivery of a thing): real contracts;
- verbis (by words): the stipulatio;
- litteris (by writing): the literal contract;
- consensu (by agreement alone): consensual contracts.
Justinian adds obligations arising 'as if from contract' (quasi ex contractu, e.g. unjustified enrichment, unauthorised administration) and 'as if from delict' (quasi ex delicto).

Real contracts
These were formed by handing over a thing, and the obligation was to return it.
- Mutuum: a loan for consumption of fungibles (money, grain, wine). Ownership passes to the borrower, who must return the same quantity of the same kind. It was enforced by the condictio. It was gratuitous, so interest required a separate stipulatio.
- Commodatum: a gratuitous loan for use. The lender keeps ownership and the borrower must return the same thing. Because the borrower alone benefits, he was held to a high standard of care.
- Depositum: gratuitous safekeeping. The depositee must return the thing on demand and, as he receives no benefit, was liable only for dolus (deliberate wrongdoing) and gross negligence.
- Pignus: delivery of a thing as security (pledge). The creditor must return it when the debt is paid.
These standards illustrate the 'utility' principle: the more a party benefits from a contract, the higher the standard of care expected of him.

The stipulatio
The stipulatio was the most versatile Roman contract.
- Form: an oral question and a matching answer between parties present together, e.g. 'Spondesne centum dare?' – 'Spondeo.' The word spondeo was reserved for citizens; other verbs could be used with foreigners.
- The answer had to correspond to the question; a mismatch could invalidate it.
- It was unilateral (only the promisor was bound) and stricti iuris: the judge enforced the words, not wider good faith.
- Its content could be almost anything lawful and possible, so any agreement could be made binding by casting it as a stipulation. It was used for loans with interest, penalty clauses, suretyship, dowry promises and novation.
- Strictness was softened by the praetor's exceptio doli (defence of fraud). Over time written records of stipulations became usual, and in AD 472 the emperor Leo relaxed the requirement of formal words.

The literal contract
In classical law, an entry in a Roman's account books (transcriptio nominum) could create a debt by converting an existing obligation into a literal one. By Justinian's time this had disappeared, and the literal contract is presented as arising from a written acknowledgment of debt.

Innominate contracts and pacts
- An agreement for exchange or other reciprocal performance ('I give so that you give', do ut des, and similar) was not one of the named contracts. Once one party had performed, the classical law gave him a condictio to recover what he had given; later law developed the actio praescriptis verbis to enforce the counter-performance. These are called innominate contracts. Barter (permutatio) is the main example.
- A bare pact (nudum pactum) did not create an action: 'a bare agreement does not give rise to an obligation but gives rise to a defence' (Ulpian). Some pacts were enforced, such as pacts attached to good-faith contracts and certain pacts recognised by the praetor or emperors.

Exam tips: when asked whether an agreement is enforceable, first classify it among the named contracts, then consider stipulatio, innominate contracts and pacts. Always identify the required form and the action that enforces it.

notes.h: Consensual contracts: sale, hire, partnership and mandate
notes.body:
The four consensual contracts were formed by agreement alone, without any form or delivery. They were enforced by good-faith actions (iudicia bonae fidei), in which the judge assessed what each party owed the other in good faith. Many historians regard them as Roman law's most 'modern' achievement.

Sale (emptio venditio)
Formation requires agreement on the thing (merx) and the price (pretium).
- The price must be in money. The Sabinians thought barter could be sale; the Proculians disagreed, and their view prevailed (Justinian's Institutes 3.23.2). Barter therefore became an innominate contract.
- The price must be certain (or ascertainable) and genuine, not a sham disguising a gift.
- A text in Justinian's Code (C.4.44.2, in the name of Diocletian) allowed a seller of land for less than half its true value to rescind unless the buyer made up the price. This doctrine, later called laesio enormis, is widely thought to be a Justinianic interpolation.
- Arra (earnest money) could evidence the agreement.

Risk
Once the sale was 'perfect' (the thing identified, price fixed, any condition fulfilled), risk of accidental destruction passed to the buyer even before delivery: periculum est emptoris. The buyer must still pay. The seller remained liable for his own fault and was expected to look after the thing (custodia) until delivery.

The seller's duties
- To deliver vacant possession (vacuam possessionem tradere). Notably, the seller was not obliged to make the buyer owner; he had to give undisturbed possession and guarantee against eviction.
- Eviction: originally protected by the actio auctoritatis (for mancipatio) and by stipulations for double the price (stipulatio duplae). Later the buyer could sue on the sale itself (actio empti) if evicted.
- Latent defects: the curule aediles' edict, governing sales of slaves and animals in the market, required disclosure of certain defects. It gave the buyer the actio redhibitoria (rescission, within six months) or the actio quanti minoris (price reduction, within a year). In Justinian's law these remedies applied to sales of all kinds of property (the Digest says so, D.21.1.1 pr and D.21.1.63); the usual view is that this generalisation reflects Justinian's compilers, though some scholars think it began earlier. Separately, a seller who knowingly concealed a defect was liable under the actio empti.

Mistake
Error as to the identity of the thing prevented agreement. Ulpian held a sale void for mistake as to the substance, e.g. vinegar sold as wine, or bronze as gold.

Hire (locatio conductio)
One contract covering three situations, always for a money payment (merces):
- locatio conductio rei: hire of a thing (land, a house, a slave);
- locatio conductio operarum: hire of services (labour);
- locatio conductio operis faciendi: a contract for a piece of work (e.g. building a house or cleaning clothes), where the contractor (conductor) undertakes a result.
Craftsmen such as fullers and tailors who took in goods were strictly liable for their safekeeping (custodia).

Partnership (societas)
An agreement to pool resources or efforts for a common purpose.
- Each partner shares profits and losses as agreed, or equally; an arrangement giving one partner all profit and none of the loss (societas leonina, the 'lion's share') was invalid.
- Partners owed the care they took in their own affairs (diligentia quam suis rebus).
- It ended on death, renunciation or completion of the purpose. Judgment in the actio pro socio carried infamy.

Mandate (mandatum)
A gratuitous undertaking by the mandatary to carry out a task for the mandator, who must reimburse expenses.
- Gratuitousness was essential; if payment was agreed, the contract was hire.
- A mandate solely in the mandatary's own interest ('do this for your own benefit') was mere advice and not binding.
- It ended on the death of either party or on revocation or renunciation.

Exam tips: in sale problems work in order: is there a valid sale (thing, price, consent)? When did risk pass? What duties did the seller break (possession, eviction, defects)? Which action is available?

Delict, the Faculty notes, is the Roman concept of wrongful conduct, ancestor of the modern law of tort and delict. Gaius (3.182) names four delicts: theft (furtum), robbery (rapina), wrongful damage to property (damnum iniuria datum) and insult (iniuria). Wrongful damage was governed by the lex Aquilia.

The statute
The lex Aquilia was a plebiscite, traditionally dated to around 287 BC. It had three chapters:
- Chapter 1: whoever wrongfully killed another's slave or four-footed herd animal (pecus, e.g. cattle, horses, sheep) must pay the highest value the thing had in the previous year.
- Chapter 2: an adstipulator (a secondary creditor) who released the debt in fraud of the principal creditor; this chapter fell out of use.
- Chapter 3: for other damage to property, by burning, breaking or rending (urere, frangere, rumpere), the wrongdoer paid the value in the next thirty days. 'Rumpere' was interpreted broadly as 'corrumpere', to spoil, covering almost any physical damage, including wounding slaves and animals.
A defendant who denied liability and lost paid double.

The requirements
1. Damage to a thing (or loss of a slave or animal) belonging to the claimant. Only the owner could originally sue; the praetor extended actions to others, such as usufructuaries and good-faith possessors.
2. Causation in the right way. The statute required the defendant to kill or damage by his own body, directly to the thing (corpore corpori). For example, administering poison by force counted as killing, while handing it over for the victim to take did not. Where harm was caused indirectly, such as shutting up a slave so that he starved, or the defendant's act merely created the occasion of the loss, the praetor gave an actio in factum (or actio utilis) instead.
3. Iniuria: originally 'without right' (e.g. not in self-defence). The jurists developed it into a requirement of fault, either intention (dolus) or negligence (culpa). Ulpian said that even the slightest fault counts under the lex Aquilia.

Fault in the cases
- The pruner (Paul, D.9.2.31): a man cutting branches from a tree drops one on a passing slave. He is liable if he did not shout a warning near a public path, and, as Quintus Mucius held, also on private land where people commonly pass. Culpa is defined there as failing to foresee what a diligent person could have foreseen, or giving warning only when it was too late to avoid the danger.
- The javelin throwers (Ulpian, D.9.2.9.4): if a slave crosses a field while others are practising with javelins there and is killed, his owner has no Aquilian claim, because the slave should not have crossed at such a time; but anyone who deliberately aims at him is liable. Justinian's Institutes (4.3.4) add that a soldier practising on a training ground is not at fault, whereas anyone else, or a soldier practising somewhere not set aside for it, is.
- The barber (Ulpian, D.9.2.11 pr): a ball hit hard during a game knocks a barber's hand while he shaves a slave in a public place, and the slave's throat is cut. The barber may be liable for working where people play; but someone who chooses to be shaved in a dangerous place has himself to blame.
- The mule driver (Institutes 4.3.8): a driver who cannot hold back his mules through inexperience, or through weakness where a stronger man could have held them, is liable. This applies the rule stated just before (Institutes 4.3.7, of an unskilled doctor) that lack of skill counts as fault (imperitia culpae adnumeratur).
- Defences included self-defence and necessity, e.g. pulling down a neighbour's house to stop a fire spreading.

Injuries to free persons
A free person is not owned ('no one is regarded as owner of his own limbs'), so the statute did not cover him directly. The jurists gave the injured free person an actio utilis (and a father could sue for injury to a son in his power), covering medical expenses and lost earnings. Texts on injuries to free persons add that scars and disfigurement are not valued, since a free body has no price (e.g. D.9.3.7).

Assessment and nature
Because the valuation could exceed actual loss, the action was partly penal, though the jurists moved it towards compensation, including consequential losses.

Legacy
The Aquilian action became the civilian basis of liability for negligent damage, influencing the French Code civil (art. 1382, now art. 1240) and the BGB (§ 823); South African law still uses it.

Exam tips: in problem questions take each element in turn (which chapter, damage, causation and form of action, fault, quantum). Cite the classic Digest cases by name.

Alongside wrongful damage, the Romans recognised theft, robbery and insult as delicts, together with a group of 'quasi-delicts'. Delictal actions were largely penal: they punished the wrongdoer, often by a multiple of the value, and could be combined with actions to recover the property.

Theft (furtum)
Paul's definition, repeated in Justinian's Institutes (4.1.1): theft is the fraudulent handling (contrectatio) of a thing with a view to gain, whether of the thing itself, or of its use or possession.
- Contrectatio (handling) was wide: it covered not only taking the thing away, but any dishonest dealing with it.
- Fraudulent intent was required: someone who took a thing believing the owner would consent did not commit theft.
- Furtum usus: a borrower or depositee who used the thing in a way not permitted, e.g. riding a borrowed horse further than agreed.
- Furtum possessionis: even an owner could commit theft by removing his own thing from a pledge creditor's possession.
Penalties (classical law):
- furtum manifestum (thief caught in the act): fourfold the value;
- furtum nec manifestum: double the value.
The Twelve Tables had punished the manifest thief far more severely; the praetor replaced this with the fourfold penalty.
Who could sue: the person with an interest in the thing's safety, not necessarily the owner. For example, a fuller or tailor who was strictly liable for the customer's goods, and so bore the loss, had the actio furti.
The penal actio furti was cumulative with the owner's rei vindicatio or the condictio furtiva to recover the thing or its value.

Robbery (rapina)
Theft with violence. The praetor introduced the actio vi bonorum raptorum (1st century BC), for fourfold the value if brought within a year (single value afterwards). The fourfold sum included the value of the thing itself.

Insult (iniuria)
Iniuria in this sense was an intentional affront to a person's body, dignity or reputation (corpus, dignitas, fama).
- The Twelve Tables set fixed penalties, including retaliation (talio) for a broken limb unless the parties settled, and small money penalties for lesser blows. Aulus Gellius tells of Lucius Veratius, who amused himself by slapping passers-by and having a slave pay the fixed 25 asses on the spot, because inflation had made the penalty trivial.
- The praetor replaced fixed penalties with the actio iniuriarum aestimatoria, in which the judge assessed a sum according to the circumstances. Serious (atrox) iniuria, depending on the act, the place or the victim's status, attracted higher sums.
- Iniuria covered assaults, defamatory shouting (convicium), following respectable women and interfering with a person's use of public places.
- Intention to insult (animus iniuriandi) was required. A paterfamilias could sue for insults to his children or wife, because the insult touched him too.

Quasi-delicts
Justinian's Institutes (4.5) list four liabilities arising 'as if from delict', often strict or for the acts of others:
- the judge who 'made the case his own' (iudex qui litem suam facit), e.g. by deciding wrongly through fault or corruption;
- things thrown or poured from a building onto a public way (actio de effusis vel deiectis): the occupier was liable for double the damage, a fixed sum for killing a free person, and what the judge thought fair for injuring one;
- things placed or hung dangerously over a public way (positum vel suspensum): a penalty recoverable by anyone;
- shipowners, innkeepers and stablekeepers liable for theft or damage by their employees on their premises.

Noxal liability
A paterfamilias or master was liable for delicts committed by his son or slave. He could either pay the penalty or surrender the wrongdoer to the victim (noxae deditio). Liability followed the wrongdoer if he changed hands ('noxa caput sequitur'). Damage by animals gave the actio de pauperie, from the Twelve Tables, again with the option of surrendering the animal.

Exam tips: in theft problems, check handling, fraudulent intent and the gain element, then decide whether the theft was manifest and who has the interest to sue. Remember that the penal and the recovery actions run together.

cards.b: c. 451–450 BC, drafted by the decemviri: the first written statement of Roman law.
Elementary textbook c. AD 161, the only classical legal work surviving substantially intact; rediscovered in a Verona palimpsest in 1816.
All law relates to persons, things or actions.

cards.f: The four parts of Justinian's codification
cards.b: Digest (50 books of juristic extracts, 533), Institutes (533), Code (2nd ed. 534) and Novels (later legislation).
An alteration of a classical text made by Justinian's compilers when excerpting it for the Digest or Code.
Caracalla's grant of Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.
The revival of the Digest from the late 11th century (Bologna, glossators, Accursius' Glossa) and its spread as the European ius commune, later shaping the Code civil (1804) and the BGB (1900).

cards.f: Sources of law listed by Gaius (1.2)
cards.b: Leges, plebiscita, senatusconsulta, imperial constitutions, edicts of magistrates, and responsa of jurists.
Made plebiscites binding on all citizens, so statutes of the plebeian assembly (like the lex Aquilia) became general law.
Law created by magistrates' edicts, mainly the praetor's, to aid, supplement or correct the civil law (Papinian).
Under Hadrian (c. AD 130) the jurist Julian settled the text of the praetor's edict, which then became fixed.
Right granted by Augustus to selected jurists to give opinions backed by the emperor's authority.
Directed judges to follow the majority of Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Modestinus and Gaius; Papinian prevailed on a tie.
Two stages: in iure before the praetor, who issued a written formula, and apud iudicem before a lay judge who decided the case.
Demonstratio (facts), intentio (claim), condemnatio (power to condemn or absolve), and sometimes an exceptio (defence).
Italian land and buildings, slaves, oxen, horses, mules, donkeys, and rustic praedial servitudes.
Formal transfer of res mancipi before at least five adult citizen witnesses and a scale-holder (libripens), with a set formula and the striking of the scale with bronze.
Informal delivery of possession with a iusta causa; transferred ownership of res nec mancipi (and, under Justinian, of all things).
Holding a res mancipi delivered without mancipatio; protected by the praetor (exceptio rei venditae et traditae, actio Publiciana) until usucapio made it full ownership.
Res habilis, titulus (iusta causa), fides (good faith), possessio, tempus.
Twelve Tables: 2 years for land, 1 year for other things. Justinian: 3 years for movables; 10 or 20 years for land.
The owner's action to recover his thing from the person possessing it; requires proof of ownership.
Praetorian action treating a claimant in the course of usucapio as if the period had run; protects bonitary owners and good-faith acquirers from non-owners (the latter not against the true owner).
Acquisition of a res nullius (e.g. a wild animal, an abandoned thing) by taking it; ownership of a wild animal ends when it regains its natural freedom.
Trebatius: the hunter owns it while pursuing; the prevailing view, followed by Justinian: only when actually captured.
Treasure found on one's own land goes to the finder; found by chance on another's land, half to the finder and half to the landowner.
Whatever is built on land belongs to the owner of the land.
The board goes with the painting (a painting by Apelles should not accede to a cheap board), with compensation to the board's owner.
If the new thing can be reduced to its materials, the materials' owner owns it; if not, the maker; if the maker used partly his own materials, the maker.
Uti possidetis (land), utrubi (movables), unde vi (forcible ejection): protect possession regardless of ownership.
Personal servitude: the right to use another's thing and take its fruits without impairing its substance; ends at the latest on the holder's death.
A legal bond by which we are bound by necessity to perform something according to the laws of our state.
Re (real), verbis (stipulatio), litteris (literal), consensu (consensual).
Loan for consumption of fungibles; ownership passes; borrower returns equivalent quantity and kind; enforced by condictio; interest needs a separate stipulatio.
Commodatum: gratuitous loan for use, borrower benefits so high standard of care. Depositum: gratuitous safekeeping, depositee liable only for dolus and gross negligence.
Oral contract by matching question and answer between parties present ('Spondesne?' – 'Spondeo'); unilateral and stricti iuris.
A bare agreement does not create an obligation but can give rise to a defence (Ulpian).
Reciprocal agreements outside the named types (e.g. barter) that became enforceable once one party had performed (condictio; later actio praescriptis verbis).

cards.f: Utility principle for standards of care
cards.b: The more a party benefits from a contract, the stricter the standard of care: borrower in commodatum high, depositee low.
Agreement (consent) on the thing sold (merx) and a certain, genuine price in money (pretium).
Proculians held barter was not sale because the price must be money; their view prevailed (Institutes 3.23.2), making barter an innominate contract.
Once a sale is perfect, the risk of accidental loss passes to the buyer, who must pay even if the thing perishes before delivery.
To deliver vacant possession and guarantee against eviction; not, in principle, to transfer ownership.
Actio redhibitoria (rescission, 6 months) and actio quanti minoris (price reduction, 1 year) for undisclosed defects, originally in market sales of slaves and animals.
Rule in C.4.44.2 (attributed to Diocletian, probably interpolated) allowing a seller of land for under half its value to rescind unless the buyer pays the shortfall.
Rei (hire of a thing), operarum (hire of services) and operis faciendi (a piece of work contracted for a result).
A partnership in which one partner takes all profits and bears no losses: invalid.
Wrongful killing of another's slave or four-footed herd animal: liability for the highest value in the preceding year.
Other damage by burning, breaking or rending (rumpere, read as 'corrumpere'): liability for the value within the next 30 days.
The statutory action required damage caused directly by the defendant's body to the thing; indirect causation gave only an actio in factum.

cards.f: Meaning of iniuria in the lex Aquilia
cards.b: Originally 'without right'; developed by the jurists into fault (dolus or culpa); Ulpian: even the slightest fault counts.
Pruner who drops a branch on a passer-by near a path without shouting a warning is liable; culpa is failure to foresee what a diligent person could foresee (Q. Mucius).
Ball knocks a barber's hand while shaving a slave in a public place; barber may be liable, but one who is shaved in a dangerous place has himself to blame.
Lack of skill counts as fault (Inst. 4.3.7, of an unskilled doctor); applied in Inst. 4.3.8 to a mule driver who cannot control his mules through inexperience.

cards.f: Penalty for denial under the lex Aquilia
cards.b: A defendant who denied liability and lost was condemned in double (lis infitiando crescit in duplum).
The fraudulent handling (contrectatio) of a thing for gain, whether of the thing itself, its use, or its possession.

cards.f: Penalties for theft in classical law
cards.b: Furtum manifestum (caught in the act): fourfold; furtum nec manifestum: double.
Theft of use: e.g. a borrower of a horse who rides it further than agreed.

cards.f: Who could bring the actio furti?
cards.b: The person with an interest in the thing's safety (e.g. a fuller strictly liable for customers' clothes), not necessarily the owner.
Praetorian action for robbery: fourfold the value within a year (single value afterwards), including the value of the thing.
Praetorian action for insult in which the judge assessed a sum appropriate to the circumstances, replacing the fixed Twelve Tables penalties.
Slapped passers-by and had a slave pay the fixed 25-as penalty on the spot, showing why the praetor replaced fixed penalties for iniuria.
Quasi-delict: occupier liable for things thrown or poured onto a public way; double damages for property, a fixed sum for killing a free person.
A master or paterfamilias liable for a slave's or son's delict could pay or surrender the wrongdoer (noxae deditio); liability followed the wrongdoer.

questions.q: Which work is the only classical Roman legal text to survive substantially in its original form?
questions.why: Gaius' Institutes survived in a Verona palimpsest. The Digest is a 6th-century compilation of excerpts (with interpolations); the Twelve Tables survive only in fragments quoted by later writers; the Theodosian Code is a 5th-century collection of imperial constitutions, not a classical juristic work.

questions.q: In which year did Justinian's Digest come into force?
questions.why: The Digest and Institutes came into force at the end of 533. 212 is the Constitutio Antoniniana, 438 the Theodosian Code, and 1804 the French Code civil.

questions.q: In what senses can Roman law be described as an 'advanced' legal system? Give specific examples.
markScheme: Professional jurists developing law through reasoned case analysis
Contracts formed by consent alone (consensual contracts) and good faith standards
Objective fault standard (culpa) under the lex Aquilia
Abstract concepts: ownership distinguished from possession; obligations as legal bonds
Acknowledges limits/alien features (slavery, patria potestas, penal delicts, formalism)
questions.modelAnswer: Roman law was advanced because it was developed by a class of professional jurists who reasoned from concrete cases to general principles, producing a body of law later systematised by Gaius and Justinian. It recognised contracts formed by consent alone (sale, hire, partnership, mandate), enforced through actions in which the judge assessed what good faith required. The lex Aquilia came to impose liability for culpa, judged against what a diligent person would have foreseen, a recognisably modern idea of negligence. It drew abstract distinctions, such as between ownership (dominium) and possession, and defined an obligation as a legal bond binding someone to perform. Its method and vocabulary were later received across Europe. But it also had features alien to modern law: slavery, the extensive power of the paterfamilias, a penal approach to delict, and early formalism (mancipatio, stipulatio).

questions.q: Which magistrate was created c. 242 BC to deal with cases involving foreigners?
questions.why: The praetor peregrinus handled disputes involving non-citizens and contributed to the ius gentium. The praetor urbanus dates from 367 BC; the curule aediles supervised markets and issued an edict on sales; the censor kept the citizen register.

questions.q: In the formulary system, who decided the facts and gave judgment?
options: A jurist with the ius respondendi
A lay judge (iudex) appointed for the case
questions.why: The praetor only framed the issue in a formula (in iure); a private lay iudex then heard evidence and condemned or absolved. The emperor's courts belong to the later cognitio procedure, and jurists advised but did not decide cases.

questions.q: Explain the role of the praetor's edict in the development of Roman private law.
markScheme: Praetor controlled access to remedies and published an annual edict
Created new actions and exceptions, e.g. actio Publiciana, defences of fraud
Papinian: to aid, supplement or correct the civil law
Edict carried forward year to year; fixed by Julian under Hadrian
Result: ius honorarium alongside ius civile; flexibility without legislation
questions.modelAnswer: The praetor, as the magistrate in charge of civil litigation, decided which actions and defences to grant. At the start of his year he published an edict announcing the remedies he would give, and successive praetors carried forward clauses that worked, so the edict accumulated into a body of law. Through it the praetors could create new actions, such as the actio Publiciana protecting a person in the course of usucapio, and exceptions such as the defence of fraud, without any legislation. Papinian described this law as introduced to aid, supplement or correct the civil law in the public interest. The result was the ius honorarium, which existed alongside the ius civile and often prevailed in practice. Under Hadrian, Salvius Julianus settled the text of the edict, ending its free development, and further change came mainly through the jurists and imperial legislation.

questions.q: In classical law, A delivers a slave to B by traditio following a sale. Which statement is correct?
options: B holds the slave in bonis and can become civil owner by usucapio
B can never acquire ownership of a slave
questions.why: A slave is a res mancipi, so traditio does not transfer civil ownership; B has bonitary ownership protected by the praetor and acquires full ownership after usucapio (one year for movables in classical law). The transaction is not void, and slaves could be owned.

questions.q: Which of the following could NOT be acquired by usucapio?
options: A horse bought in good faith from a non-owner
A stolen cloak bought in good faith
Land bought from a non-owner in good faith
Res mancipi delivered by traditio after sale
questions.why: Stolen things were excluded from usucapio by the Twelve Tables and the lex Atinia, even in the hands of a good-faith purchaser. The other cases are classic examples of usucapio curing a defect in title.

questions.q: Explain the requirements of usucapio and the purposes it served in Roman law.
markScheme: Lists res habilis, iusta causa, bona fides, possessio, tempus
Stolen and forcibly taken things excluded (Twelve Tables, lex Atinia)
Periods in classical law and under Justinian
Purpose: curing defects of form (res mancipi by traditio)
Purpose: curing defects of title (purchase from non-owner) and easing proof of ownership
questions.modelAnswer: Usucapio was acquisition of ownership by possession for a set time. The requirements were: a thing capable of usucapio (stolen things and things taken by force were excluded by the Twelve Tables and later statutes such as the lex Atinia); a lawful ground of acquisition (iusta causa, e.g. sale or gift); good faith at the outset; actual possession; and the required period, which was one year for movables and two for land in classical law, and three years for movables and ten or twenty for land under Justinian. It served two main purposes. It cured defects of form, for example where a res mancipi had been delivered by traditio rather than mancipatio. It also cured defects of title, as where the acquirer bought from a non-owner in good faith. More generally it gave certainty, since an owner seeking to vindicate needed to prove ownership, which usucapio made far easier.

questions.q: B makes wine from grapes belonging to A, without A's consent, using only A's grapes. Under Justinian's view, who owns the wine?
options: A, because he owned the materials
B, because the wine cannot be turned back into grapes
questions.why: Justinian's middle view gives the new thing to the maker where it cannot be reduced to its original materials, as with wine from grapes. A would own it on the Sabinian view, and A could still have a personal remedy (and B may be liable for theft if dishonest). Common ownership arises from consensual mixtures, not specificatio.

questions.q: C, a hunter, wounds a wild boar and is chasing it when D catches it. On the view adopted in Justinian's Institutes:
options: C owns it because he wounded it first
C and D own it in common
D owns it because ownership requires capture
questions.why: Justinian followed the majority view that a wild animal becomes yours only when you capture it, because much can happen to prevent capture. Trebatius' contrary view (ownership while pursuit continues) was rejected. Landowners could forbid entry but did not own wild animals on their land.

questions.q: Explain the Sabinian, Proculian and Justinianic views on specificatio, and apply them to a bronze statue made by B from A's bronze.
markScheme: Defines specificatio (new thing made from another's materials)
Sabinian: owner of materials
Proculian: maker
Justinian: reducible to materials → materials' owner; otherwise maker; maker's own materials partly → maker
Application: statue can be melted down, so A owns it under Justinian (and Sabinians); B under Proculians
questions.modelAnswer: Specificatio is the making of a new thing (nova species) from materials owned by another. The Sabinians held that the new thing belongs to the owner of the materials, as the substance remains his. The Proculians held that it belongs to the maker, since the new thing did not exist before and he created it. Justinian adopted a middle view: if the new thing can be reduced to its former materials, it belongs to the materials' owner; if it cannot, it belongs to the maker; and if the maker used partly his own materials, he owns the product. A bronze statue can be melted back into bronze, so under the Justinianic and Sabinian views A owns the statue, while on the Proculian view B, the maker, would own it.

questions.q: A lends B ten jars of wine, to be repaid with ten jars of similar wine next year. This is:
questions.why: Mutuum is a loan for consumption of fungibles, returning the same quantity and kind, with ownership passing to the borrower. Commodatum and depositum require return of the very same thing; pignus is a pledge as security.

questions.q: Which statement about the stipulatio is correct?
options: It required a corresponding oral question and answer between parties present
It could only be used for sales
questions.why: The stipulatio was an oral contract formed by a question and corresponding answer between parties present together. Writing became customary as evidence but was not the essence. It was unilateral, binding only the promisor, and could be used for almost any lawful promise.

questions.q: Why was the stipulatio so important in Roman law? Refer to its form and uses.
markScheme: Form: oral question and congruent answer, parties present, spondeo for citizens
Unilateral and strict (stricti iuris)
Flexible content: any lawful, possible promise could be made binding
Uses: interest, penalty clauses, suretyship, novation, dowry
Softening: exceptio doli; written evidence; Leo's reform AD 472
questions.modelAnswer: The stipulatio was formed by an oral question by the creditor and a corresponding answer by the promisor, with both present, e.g. 'Spondesne?' – 'Spondeo' (a verb reserved to citizens). It was unilateral and stricti iuris: the promisor was bound by the words and the judge did not look to wider good faith. Its importance came from its flexibility. Because its content could be any lawful and possible performance, it allowed Romans to make binding agreements that did not fit any named contract, overcoming the rule that bare pacts were not actionable. It was used for loans with interest, penalty clauses, suretyship, promises of dowry and novation of existing debts. Its harshness was moderated by the praetor's exceptio doli, and later written records were treated as evidence of the oral exchange; in AD 472 Leo removed the need for particular formal words.

questions.q: A agrees to sell B a specific slave for 1,000 sesterces. Before delivery, without A's fault, the slave dies. Under Roman law:
options: The sale is void and B need not pay
B must still pay, because risk passed when the sale was perfected
questions.why: Under the rule periculum est emptoris, risk passes to the buyer once the sale is perfect (thing identified, price fixed), so B must pay. A is liable only if he was at fault. Specific goods cannot be replaced by substitutes, and risk is tied to perfection of the sale, not to the conveyance.

questions.q: A agrees to clean B's cloak for a fee. The contract is:
questions.why: A paid undertaking to produce a result (a cleaned cloak) is locatio conductio operis faciendi. Mandate must be gratuitous; partnership requires a common purpose and sharing of profit; commodatum is a gratuitous loan for use.

questions.q: Outline the seller's obligations in Roman sale and the buyer's remedies for eviction and latent defects.
markScheme: Seller must deliver vacant possession; not bound to transfer ownership
Custodia/care until delivery; liability for fault
Eviction: actio auctoritatis/stipulatio duplae, later actio empti
Aedilician edict: disclosure; actio redhibitoria (6 months) and quanti minoris (1 year)
Remedies available for all sales in Justinian's law (usually seen as a Justinianic generalisation); actio empti for knowing concealment (dolus)
Good-faith nature of actio empti
questions.modelAnswer: The seller's basic duty was to deliver vacant possession (vacuam possessionem tradere) and to look after the thing until delivery, being liable for his fault. He was not bound, as such, to make the buyer owner, but he guaranteed that the buyer would not be evicted by someone with better title. Originally this guarantee came from the actio auctoritatis where the thing was mancipated, or from a stipulation for double the price (stipulatio duplae). Later the buyer evicted could sue on the sale itself by the actio empti, a good-faith action. For latent defects, the curule aediles' edict required sellers of slaves and animals in the market to disclose certain defects and gave the buyer the actio redhibitoria to undo the sale within six months or the actio quanti minoris to reduce the price within a year. In Justinian's law the remedies applied to sales of every kind, a generalisation usually attributed to the compilers. A seller who knowingly concealed a defect was liable under the actio empti for the buyer's loss.

questions.q: D hands poison to A's slave, who drinks it believing it is medicine and dies. Under classical law, A's remedy is:
options: An actio in factum, because D did not kill corpore corpori
No remedy, because the slave drank voluntarily
questions.why: Handing poison to someone who then takes it causes death indirectly ('furnishing a cause of death'), so the praetor granted an actio in factum rather than the direct statutory action, which required killing by direct bodily force. Theft is irrelevant, and the slave's ignorance means he did not voluntarily accept the risk.

questions.q: Under chapter 3 of the lex Aquilia, damages were assessed as:
options: The highest value in the past year
The value in the next thirty days
Double the actual loss in all cases
questions.why: Chapter 3 used the value within the next thirty days (interpreted to mean the highest value). The past year applies to chapter 1. Double applied only if the defendant denied liability and lost; fourfold relates to manifest theft and robbery.

questions.q: How did the Roman jurists develop the concept of fault (culpa) under the lex Aquilia? Refer to specific cases.
markScheme: Iniuria originally meant 'without right'; developed into fault
Culpa as failure to foresee what a diligent person could (Paul, pruner D.9.2.31)
Context-sensitive: javelin field (D.9.2.9.4; Inst. 4.3.4)
Victim's own fault: barber case (D.9.2.11 pr)
Lack of skill as fault (mule driver); Ulpian's 'levissima culpa'
questions.modelAnswer: The statute required damage done iniuria, which originally meant without legal justification. The jurists turned this into a requirement of fault: intention (dolus) or negligence (culpa), and Ulpian said even the slightest fault sufficed. They developed an objective standard through cases. In the pruner case (D.9.2.31) Paul held a man who dropped a branch on a passer-by liable if he failed to shout a warning near a public path, and reported Quintus Mucius' definition of culpa as failing to foresee what a diligent person could have foreseen. The standard depended on context: javelin throwers were not liable when a slave rashly crossed the field where they were practising, though a deliberate throw at him was (D.9.2.9.4), and the Institutes treat practising outside a proper training ground as culpable (Inst. 4.3.4). In the barber case (D.9.2.11 pr) the jurists weighed the barber's choice of a dangerous place against the customer's own fault in submitting to be shaved there. Lack of skill also counted as fault, as with the inexperienced mule driver (Inst. 4.3.8). The result resembles the modern reasonable person standard.

questions.q: B borrows A's horse to ride to a nearby town but, without permission, rides it to a distant city. This is:
options: No delict, since B had A's consent to use the horse
questions.why: Using a borrowed thing in a way the owner did not permit is theft of use (furtum usus), provided B knew A would not consent. Rapina requires violence; damnum iniuria datum requires physical damage to the horse.

questions.q: A thief is caught in the act of carrying off C's silver. In classical law, C's penal action is for:
questions.why: Furtum manifestum carried a fourfold penalty under the praetor's edict. Double was for non-manifest theft. The Twelve Tables' harsher personal penalties for the manifest thief had been replaced by the classical period. C could also recover the silver itself by vindicatio or its value by condictio furtiva.

questions.q: Explain the Roman delict of iniuria and how it developed from the Twelve Tables to the praetorian action.
markScheme: Iniuria as intentional affront to body, dignity or reputation
Twelve Tables fixed penalties (talio for broken limb, small money penalties)
Inflation made penalties trivial: Lucius Veratius story
Praetor's actio iniuriarum aestimatoria: judge assesses sum; atrox iniuria
Extended to defamatory shouting, following women etc.; animus iniuriandi; paterfamilias may sue
questions.modelAnswer: Iniuria was an intentional affront to a person's body, dignity or reputation. The Twelve Tables dealt mainly with physical attacks, imposing retaliation for a broken limb unless the parties settled, and fixed money penalties for lesser blows. As the value of money fell, these fixed penalties became trivial. Aulus Gellius' story of Lucius Veratius, who slapped passers-by and had a slave pay the 25 asses at once, illustrates the problem. The praetor responded with the actio iniuriarum aestimatoria, in which the judge assessed a sum appropriate to the circumstances, with higher sums for atrox iniuria, judged by the act, place or the victim's status. The praetor's edict also extended the delict to non-physical affronts, such as defamatory public shouting and following respectable women. Intention to insult was required, and a paterfamilias could sue for insults to members of his household.

questions.q: Titius is pruning a tree overhanging a path in Seius' private garden, which Seius allows neighbours to use as a shortcut. Without shouting a warning, he drops a heavy branch, which (a) kills Stichus, a slave belonging to Maevius, who is walking along the path, and (b) breaks an amphora of wine carried by Stichus, which belongs to Sempronia. Frightened by the crash, Maevius' horse, tethered nearby, bolts into a ditch and breaks its leg. Discuss the liability of Titius under the lex Aquilia.
markScheme: Identifies the lex Aquilia elements: damage, causation corpore corpori, iniuria/culpa, and the claimant's standing
Stichus: chapter 1 (slave killed), direct killing by bodily force; quantum highest value in past year
Fault: pruner case (D.9.2.31): failure to shout warning; whether the path is one where people pass (private garden used as shortcut) affects foreseeability
Amphora: chapter 3 (breaking, frangere); Sempronia as owner sues; value in next 30 days
Horse: chapter 3 injury, but caused indirectly (fright), so actio in factum rather than direct action
Considers defences / contributory fault and denial doubling
Notes the actio utilis/in factum extension and Maevius' standing as owner
Clear conclusion on each head
questions.modelAnswer:
The lex Aquilia required (i) loss to a thing owned by the claimant, (ii) caused in the way the statute required, (iii) iniuria, which the jurists interpreted as fault (dolus or culpa), and (iv) gave a measure of damages depending on the chapter.

Stichus. Killing another's slave falls under chapter 1. Maevius, as owner, is the proper claimant. The branch fell from Titius' own act directly onto Stichus, so this is killing corpore corpori and the direct action lies. The key issue is fault. In the pruner case (D.9.2.31) Paul holds a pruner liable if he drops a branch near a public way without shouting a warning, culpa being failure to foresee what a diligent person could have foreseen. Following Quintus Mucius, the text adds that it matters little whether the path is public or private, since people commonly pass through private places; only where there is no path at all is liability limited to dolus. Here Seius' garden is private, but it is used as a shortcut, so passers-by were foreseeable and a diligent person would have shouted. Titius is therefore at fault, and Ulpian's statement that even slight fault suffices reinforces this. Maevius recovers the highest value Stichus had in the previous year, doubled if Titius denies liability and loses.

The amphora. Breaking (frangere) another's property falls under chapter 3. Sempronia, as owner of the amphora and wine, sues. Damage was caused directly by the branch, and the same culpa applies. She recovers the value within the next thirty days, read as the highest value in that period. The fact that the amphora was carried by someone else's slave is irrelevant to her title.

The horse. Injuring an animal is covered by chapter 3 under the broad reading of rumpere as corrumpere. However, Titius did not touch the horse; it was injured when it bolted in fright. This is causation without bodily contact, comparable to frightening an animal so that it falls, so the direct statutory action does not lie. The praetor would give Maevius an actio in factum (or utilis) on the same principles. Whether Titius is liable depends on whether a diligent person would foresee harm to animals nearby from a heavy branch falling, which is arguable, and on whether tethering a horse beside the path contributed. Roman texts such as the barber case (D.9.2.11 pr) show that a victim's own choice to expose himself or his property to danger can reduce or exclude liability.

Conclusion: Titius is very probably liable to Maevius under chapter 1 for Stichus and to Sempronia under chapter 3 for the amphora. For the horse, Maevius needs an actio in factum, and success depends on foreseeability and his own conduct.

questions.q: 'The consensual contracts were the most modern part of Roman law.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains what consensual contracts were: four types formed by consent alone
Contrasts with formal and real contracts (stipulatio, mancipatio, mutuum)
Good-faith actions (iudicia bonae fidei): judge assesses obligations, implied terms, exceptio doli inherent
Sale as example: risk rules, implied warranties of eviction and latent defects, aedilician remedies
Limits on modernity: closed list (no general contract), bare pacts unenforceable, seller not bound to transfer ownership, gratuitous mandate, slavery
Influence on civil-law codes and English law (e.g. consensual sale)
Evaluates 'most modern' against other candidates (lex Aquilia culpa, possession)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The consensual contracts were sale (emptio venditio), hire (locatio conductio), partnership (societas) and mandate (mandatum). Unlike the stipulatio, which needed a formal oral exchange, or the real contracts, which needed delivery of a thing, they were formed by agreement alone, between parties present or absent, without any form. This idea, that consent itself creates binding obligations, is the foundation of modern contract law.

Their second modern feature was the good-faith action. In iudicia bonae fidei the judge was instructed to condemn the defendant in whatever he ought to give or do in good faith. This let the jurists develop implied duties, such as the seller's guarantee against eviction and his liability for knowingly concealed defects, without express stipulations. Defences of fraud were treated as inherent in the action. Sale shows the sophistication of the rules: the parties had to agree on a certain money price, risk passed on perfection of the sale (periculum est emptoris), and the aediles' edict gave the actio redhibitoria and actio quanti minoris for undisclosed defects, which in Justinian's law applied to sales generally. Locatio conductio covered hire of things, services and work under one contract, and societas and mandatum regulated cooperation and agency-like relationships.

There are limits to the claim. Roman law never developed a general principle that every serious agreement is enforceable: the consensual contracts were a closed list, other agreements needed the form of a stipulatio or performance on one side (innominate contracts), and bare pacts gave only a defence. The seller was not bound as such to transfer ownership, only possession with a guarantee, which differs from modern sale. Mandate had to be gratuitous, reflecting social values of friendship and duty rather than commerce. Much of the context, including slaves as objects of sale and hire, is alien.

Other parts of Roman law have rival claims to modernity: the jurists' objective concept of culpa under the lex Aquilia, the protection of possession independently of ownership, and the method of reasoning from cases. But the consensual contracts were probably the most directly influential. The civil codes built their general law of contract on consent and good faith, and English law also treats sale as formed by agreement.

Overall, the statement is largely justified: the consensual contracts embodied consent and good faith, the two pillars of modern contract law. It needs qualifying, however, because they remained specific named types within a system that still relied on formality and lacked a general theory of contract.
